questions.q: Why is disabling an entire IAM account or AWS account usually the WRONG first containment move, even though it would stop the attacker?
options: AWS does not allow disabling an entire account under any circumstances
It stops every legitimate workload running in that account too, turning a contained security incident into a self-inflicted outage
It is slower than any scoped containment action
It automatically deletes CloudTrail logs
questions.explain: The goal of containment is to shrink the attacker's blast radius to near zero while leaving everything else running — reaching for the biggest lever available stops legitimate work along with the attacker.

questions.q: Why does deactivating a leaked AWS access key alone not fully contain the incident?
options: Deactivation only works on root account keys
Deactivated keys automatically reactivate after 24 hours
Deactivation requires deleting the IAM user first
A deactivated key doesn't retroactively invalidate STS temporary session tokens already issued from it before deactivation
questions.explain: Deactivating the key stops it from being used again, but any temporary credentials already issued via STS from that key remain valid until they expire or are explicitly revoked.

questions.q: How does an explicit-deny IAM policy conditioned on `aws:TokenIssueTime` help revoke active sessions from a compromised key?
options: It deletes the IAM user automatically after the deny takes effect
Because explicit denies always win, it invalidates every session token issued before the compromise timestamp, without affecting sessions issued afterward
It requires GuardDuty Enterprise to function
It only affects console sign-ins, not API calls
questions.explain: This documented AWS incident-response pattern uses the fact that an explicit Deny overrides any Allow, conditioned on the token's issue time, to cut off every session that predates detection while leaving newly rotated sessions untouched.

questions.q: Why should a compromised EC2 instance typically be isolated via a security group swap rather than terminated immediately?
options: Terminating an instance destroys the forensic evidence (memory state, disk contents) needed to understand what actually happened
Terminating an instance is always more expensive than isolating it
AWS does not allow terminating an instance that has an attached IAM role
Security groups cannot be changed on a running instance
questions.explain: Isolating the instance with a no-access security group (and snapshotting its disk) stops further damage while preserving the evidence that termination would destroy.

questions.q: Why should you remove a malicious credential from a specific Azure app registration rather than deleting the app registration entirely?
options: Azure does not allow deleting app registrations
Removing a credential requires Global Administrator, while deleting the app does not
Deleting the whole app registration would break every legitimate workload that depends on it, when only the added secret was actually malicious
App registrations cannot have their credentials removed individually
questions.explain: The scoped fix is to delete only the malicious secret that was added; deleting the entire app registration removes legitimate functionality that other systems may depend on.
